newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris suggests mediator to resolve truckers dispute.
newsitem.headline: Paris suggests mediator to resolve truckers dispute.

text.p: The French government said on Saturday a mediator should be appointed to help end a six-day protest, in which truckers have blocked about 30 towns and a dozen petrol depots.
After three rounds of talks aimed at breaking a deadlock, Transport Minister Bernard Pons said after a meeting with unions he proposed that a mediator should be appointed.

Union representatives told reporters they had accepted the offer and that Pons would put his suggestion to haulage bosses. In the meantime, unions called on truckers to continue staging blockades across the country.

The companies have agreed to allow truckers to retire at 55 instead of 60, but they want the state to foot the bill. Unions say talks are stuck over the issues of working hours and payment for all working hours, including time spent loading.

Haunted by memories of a damaging 24-day rail strike a year ago, which badly dented his popularity, Prime Minister Alain Juppe has called on both sides to end the dispute quickly and agreed that a Transport Ministry official chair the talks.

North of the south-western city of Bordeaux, which has Juppe as its mayor and is singled out for the toughest protests, truckers set up a new blockade on the A10 highway after letting dozens of exhausted Spanish, Portuguese, German and British colleagues through overnight.
Since Friday evening, truckers have virtually blocked a highway to Paris's wholesale food market at Rungis. Police said produce was getting through.

Tens of thousands of trucks blocked main roads and a dozen fuel depots. The southwest, parts of the south and the Calvados region in Normandy were all badly hit. Petrol stations ran out of fuel in areas of Normandy and in Bordeaux.
Unions say they would blockade Paris only as a last resort.
"Everything has yet to be negotiated -- working hours and wages are the biggest issues. The bosses have offered nothing," Joel Lecocq of the pro-Socialist CFDT union told reporters before the talks.
Unions said the government had agreed to finance early retirement for truckers but only on condition the talks made progress on all other sticking points.

Thousands of foreign truckers, most British and Spanish with no alternative but to drive through France, became stranded in the roadblocks, many sleeping in their cabs and running out of food and money.

The Foreign Office (foreign ministry) in London ordered consulates in France to help cashless British drivers contact their families. The Spanish embassy advised drivers to lodge complaints with the police so that they could claim compensation for rotting cargoes.
More than 1,000 British truck drivers were stuck in blockades across France and British freight operators said the dispute was ruining them.
In France, the Association of the Food Industry said the protest was also becoming a burden.
Opposition Socialist leaders spoke in support of the truckers, who say they are underpaid and overworked due to cut-throat competition between companies.
